title: How do we build a right angle at a point on a line?
description: A point O is marked on a line, and a ninety degree angle is built at O with a ruler and a compass. Equal marks on both sides make O a midpoint, and one pair of arcs gives the perpendicular bisector. Keeko's doubt, that two pairs of arcs are needed, is answered by pointing out that O already lies on the bisector.
teaching_notes: One idea: make O the midpoint of a segment X Y, and the perpendicular bisector of X Y passes through O. Watch for students who draw two pairs of arcs when one point on the bisector is already known.

source: Draw a line and mark a point O on it. Construct a 90° angle
video_script.why: The child can build a perpendicular bisector but has not used it to raise a right angle at a chosen point on a line.
video_script.substitution: Mark equal distances on both sides of O so that O is the midpoint of a segment X Y, then build the perpendicular bisector of X Y, which passes through O.
video_script.anchor: A line with a point O marked on it: construct a ninety degree angle at O with a ruler and a compass.
video_script.wrong_answer: two pairs of arcs are needed
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko draws one pair of arcs above the line and a second pair below it, as in the perpendicular bisector, before joining the points.
video_script.payoff_line: The angle eigh O X is ninety degrees

final_answer.value: ∠AOX = 90°, since ΔAOX ≅ ΔAOY by SSS and the two equal angles make a straight angle
final_answer.spoken: the angle eigh O X is ninety degrees, because the two equal angles make a straight angle

never_show: the angle AOX marked as a right angle before the last step
maths_rules: Arcs from O with one radius cut the line at X and Y: OX = OY, so O is the midpoint of XY.
Arcs of a wider radius from X and from Y meet at A above the line: AX = AY.
Triangle AOX is congruent to triangle AOY by SSS (AX = AY, OX = OY, AO common), so angle AOX = angle AOY.
Angle AOX + angle AOY = 180 degrees (straight angle), so each is 180 / 2 = 90 degrees.
Slip: a radius equal to OX from X and from Y gives arcs that meet only at O, so there is no new point above the line, or a second pair below is drawn when O is already on the bisector.
video_script.design: One idea: make O the midpoint of X Y, and the perpendicular bisector passes through O, so one pair of arcs is enough. Keeko's doubt is the book's own question, whether two pairs of arcs are needed.

<bookmark mark='m3'/>Each is half of one hundred and eighty, which is ninety degrees.
